transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Waypoint Head of AI), Marco Silva (Platform Eng), Sophie Tan (Product PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Waypoint is evaluating LLM options to power a multimodal routing assistant and customer-facing support agent. They have very large context needs (~65k tokens), need production-grade multilingual support (EN, ES, FR, DE), and want tool-calling for an internal vector DB plus authenticated calls to their logistics APIs. Security gating (SOC2, SSO, KMS) is a must for pilots.

Topics: context length, open model comparisons, quantization, hosted vs dedicated vs private, tool-calling integration, SLA and compliance requirements.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick round of intros — I'm Jordan with Redwood, AE, and with me is Priya our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Aisha: Hi, I'm Aisha, Head of AI at Waypoint, we've got Marco on platform and Sophie from product. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:15] Priya: Great. Today we wanted to riff on model choices given your constraints — you sent over the note about 65k context, multilingual, and toolcals. Is that still accurate?
[00:22] Aisha: Yeah, that's right. The main use case is a routing assistant that pulls in timeline docs and long shipment histories — so need to keep large context windows. The chat bot for customers also needs to reference multi-message threads.
[00:34] Marco: We're also pretty strict on privacy — logs go to our VPC, and any PII needs to be encrypted at rest with our KMS. We can't send certain payloads to public hosted infra without DPA and SOC2.
[00:44] Sophie: From product, we need parity of nuance in Spanish and French — our user base in EU/LatAm is big, so degraded translations are unacceptable.
[00:51] Jordan: Understood. Quick high-level: Redwood can run in hosted mode (fast onboarding), dedicated pools (predictable throughput, single-tenant GPUs), or private (customer-managed VPC or on-prem). Each has different tradeoffs for latency, cost, and control. We'll try to map model choices to those.
[01:06] Priya: If I can, I'll sketch performance tradeoffs first. For 65k context we usually look at models explicitly trained/inferred at long context — some Llama-derived models and certain Mistral branches can be configured but sometimes you need chunking + smart KV caching. Redwood's runtime supports KV cache and prefix caching, but there are unit-cost implications.
[01:26] Aisha: Are there open models that really do 65k natively without awful tokenization overhead?
[01:32] Priya: A few. There's a split: some models claim long-context support but at large memory cost. For production we recommend two patterns: 1) pick a model with native long-context support if you need single-pass reasoning across 65k, or 2) use a shorter-ctx model with RAG and a streaming KV/ prefix cache so you only materialize the working set. Both are supported in Redwood, but the former hits GPU RAM/throughput higher.
[01:50] Marco: So dedicated would help there? We can buy a larger GPU instance and pin it, right?
[01:54] Jordan: Exactly. Dedicated lets you reserve GPU pools, pass the model artifacts to the runtime, and get predictable latency. Private gives you more network control — e.g., everything inside your VPC and on-prem KMS — but increases ops overhead.
[02:07] Aisha: What's the quantization story? We want cheaper tokens but can't lose hallucination performance.
[02:12] Priya: We recommend 4-bit quant for many open models; Redwood's optimizer has tested INT4 / Q4 variants. For critical path generation we sometimes keep a float32 or float16 path, and use quantized for lower-cost branches, or for reranking. We'll send you a microbenchmark that shows latency/quality tradeoffs — some hallucination metrics nudge a bit with aggressive quantization.
[02:33] Sophie: Can you also cover tool-calling? We need model to call our vector DB (internal) and then call an authenticated REST API on our order system to change routing.
[02:42] Priya: Yes. Our function/tool calling is model-agnostic at the API layer. You can configure connector adapters — we've got patterns for a vector DB (we often see Pinecone/Weaviate/FAISS hits behind an authenticated microservice) and for outbound API calls we support signed requests via per-route secrets and can integrate with your KMS for key retrieval.
[03:00] Marco: Does that mean secrets never leave our VPC in private deployment?
[03:03] Priya: In private/on-prem, keys are customer-managed and never egress to Redwood's control plane. In dedicated/hosted, we use envelope encryption and HSM-backed KMS integrations, and you can opt for customer-managed keys with certain enterprise contracts. We'll share the security docs.
[03:16] Aisha: Good. On model accuracy for Spanish, we ran a small eval where Llama 3-ish variants did okay but struggled with domain terms; Anthropic did better on safety. Any suggestions for multilingual open models?
[03:29] Priya: Mistral and Llama-derivative multilingual fine-tuned checkpoints are decent. We also do multi-stage evaluation — base model -> multilingual finetune on your corpus -> calibrate with prompt tuning. For many customers we'll do a pilot comparing 3 candidates: 1) Large open Mistral-like that scales well for EN/FR/ES, 2) Llama-based long-context model, 3) a smaller local model with heavier retrieval.
[03:54] Sophie: How long do those pilots usually take?
[03:56] Jordan: Typical pilot is 4–6 weeks if we have sample data and clear eval prompts. Week 1: onboarding + data ingest (subset), Week 2: initial benchmarks, Week 3: model tuning + integration with tool-calls, Week 4: production-like run + cost analysis. We can extend for more thorough regression testing.
[04:12] Marco: On the integration side, how intrusive is the SDK? We use Go and Rust services.
[04:17] Priya: We have REST and SDKs in Node/Python/Go (Go is stable) — Rust community SDK is emerging. For heavy throughput we recommend the GRPC/streaming endpoint which Redwood provides in dedicated/private.
[04:29] Aisha: Can we run a stress test with our real workload? We want to simulate bursts and long-seq queries.
[04:34] Jordan: Yes, for dedicated we can set up a benchmark harness and route traffic to a reserved pool. For hosted, we can still run tests but you might see shared tenancy throttling — we can provide isolated burst windows with enterprise commit.
[04:48] Sophie: Pricing — rough ballpark for dedicated vs hosted for a 65k-context use case?
[04:54] Jordan: Ballpark varies a lot. Hosted per-token pricing for long-context is higher, and sustained 65k tokens could be costly. Dedicated is heavy capex/commit but lower per-token at scale. I'll send a sketch with example math based on expected qps and average token lengths.
[05:08] [00:05:08] Marco: I had a question — you mentioned KV cache earlier; how is that invalidated when the shipment state changes?
[05:15] Priya: Good point. We typically tie the KV/prefix cache to a session or object version. If the shipment record changes, your app can send an invalidation signal or a version token; Redwood's runtime will drop the cached prefix for that key. We can instrument hooks so your platform emits invalidation events downstream.
[05:33] Aisha: From a compliance side, we need audit logs that show which model version answered and what tool calls were issued. Do you show the full tool-call payloads in logs?
[05:42] Priya: Logs can be configured — by default we log metadata and request IDs. Full payloads can be retained in a customer-controlled storage bucket for X days if you need full audit trails. For private customers, logs never leave your control.
[05:56] Jordan: Quick aside — some transcriptions may say "case cache" instead of "KV cache" in notes; just flag that as transcription quirk.
[06:03] Aisha: (laughing) said we've got those quirks.
[06:06] [00:06:06] Sophie: On tool-calling reliability, do you have retries and fallback? If the outbound API is slow, will the model time out?
[06:13] Priya: We support pluggable policies. You can set per-route timeouts, retries, and fallback policies. For example, on API failure we can return a graceful message and fall back to a cached answer or a safe default. We surface metrics in the console so you can see latencies and error traces.
[06:29] Marco: About model governance — we have a review board that requires model lineage and drift alerts. How does Redwood help?
[06:36] Jordan: Redwood Optimize has quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. We can set up automated evals nightly against your golden prompt set and alert if quality drops. Model lineage and rollout audit is part of the console — which model version served which route and when rollouts happened.
[06:53] Aisha: Good. Any customers running similar long-context logistics use cases?
[06:57] Priya: We have a couple of logistics and supply-chain customers (anonymized) who've used long-context models for manifest history and multi-hop reasoning. They typically combine retrieval + chunking to reduce cost where native long-context models would be too expensive.
[07:12] Sophie: Are there limitations to streaming responses with 65k token history? We want users to see progressive responses.
[07:19] Priya: Streaming is supported, but with very long context there's more to compile per request which can add a pre-stream latency. We often pipeline: send initial context summary and start streaming while deeper reasoning continues, or use incremental retrieval so you can stream the first N tokens quickly.
[07:36] [00:07:36] Marco: On the private deployment end, what's the support model? We are comfortable with some ops but not running full infra.
[07:43] Jordan: Private has a customer-managed control plane option or a managed private offering. With managed private, Redwood runs updates and helps with health checks; with customer-managed you own upgrades. Both can integrate with your KMS and network.
[07:58] Aisha: We're leaning away from hosted for PII, but might use hosted for non-sensitive public docs. Does Redwood support mixed deployments?
[08:05] Priya: Yes, hybrid routing is a common pattern — sensitive requests go to dedicated/private, public samples go to hosted. Smart routing can be rules-based or ML-driven.
[08:15] Sophie: Let's talk about evaluations — what's the recommended eval matrix?
[08:19] Priya: We usually recommend: 1) Perplexity and BLEU/ROUGE aren't enough for generation; use human-in-the-loop scoring for domain correctness. 2) Latency and cost per token under representative load. 3) Safety/regression tests. 4) Multilingual parity tests per language. We'll help with an automation harness to run model A/Bs.
[08:38] Aisha: Can you mention concrete model candidates now?
[08:41] Priya: Sure — Candidate A: Mistral-xxl-style open checkpoint (good multilingual, mid-long context but needs memory). Candidate B: Llama-derivative that has been extended for long context (single-pass 64k claims). Candidate C: A retrieval-first smaller model which uses aggressive RAG and vector DB — more cost efficient but might lose holistic reasoning. We'll run these three in the pilot.
[09:02] Marco: Any red flags on license/usage? We will redistribute generated text to customers.
[09:07] Jordan: We'll check model licenses — some open checkpoints have restrictions. For hosted offering, we surface model license metadata; for dedicated/private, you manage the artifacts and licenses. We'll get legal involved on the exact redistribution terms.
[09:20] [00:09:20] Sophie: For evaluation purposes, what's the quickest path to get a baseline?
[09:24] Priya: Provide a small dataset (a dozen representative long-context threads and a dozen multilingual prompts). We'll spin up a quick hosted baseline within a week — then if you want a dedicated bench we schedule that for week 2–3.
[09:36] Aisha: Sounds good. One more: routing decisions — do you support policy-based routing by cost/latency/region?
[09:44] Jordan: Yes — smart routing can route by latency SLOs (lowest-latency region), cost thresholds, model compatibility, or customer tier. We can also set automatic fallback policies if a model becomes unavailable.
[09:58] Marco: About data retention — we need 30-day retention for logs, and immediate erasure for certain PII. Can that be done?
[10:05] Priya: Yes — configurable retention and purge APIs exist. For private deployments, you control retention; for hosted, we provide retention settings and data deletion APIs. We'll include the compliance brochure.
[10:18] [00:10:18] Jordan: Okay, let's capture next steps quickly. We'll do a 4–6 week pilot plan, Redwood to provide benchmark pack, customer to provide sample data and prompt set. We'll scope cost estimates and a dedicated pool option.
[10:29] Aisha: Can you also include a checklist of security deliverables for our procurement? They want SOC2 report, SAML SSO docs, and KMS integration details.
[10:38] Jordan: Yes — we'll add SOC2 report, SAML/SSO configuration docs, KMS/HSM integration notes, and the DPA template.
[10:46] Sophie: Can we have an SE workshop where you run one of our long threads end-to-end? Preferably week of 9/21.
[10:52] Priya: We'll block time — an hour SE-led deep bench to run real data and show tool-call flows.
[10:59] Marco: Minor transcription note: sometimes speaker labels in these exports say Speaker 3 for Marco. That's fine; we'll reconcile offline.
[11:05] Jordan: Great. Anything else before we wrap?
[11:08] Aisha: Just that licensing and the pilot budget are the main internal concerns. If you can give a low/med/high cost scenarios that helps procurement.
[11:16] Jordan: We'll do that. Priya, any last technical caveats?
[11:19] Priya: Two caveats — first, if you need true single-pass 65k reasoning we should validate memory and latency constraints on dedicated GPUs; second, quantization can help cost but always validate hallucination/regression on your eval set. We'll provide examples in the microbenchmark report.
[11:33] Sophie: Perfect. Thanks, everyone.
[11:36] Aisha: Thanks. Looking forward to the pilot.
[11:39] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and pricing.

End of call.
